desc:
Every non-empty contiguous subarray of nums has a maximum value. When the maximum occurs several times in the subarray, the leftmost occurrence is said to own the subarray. So each subarray has exactly one owner.

Return an array counts of the same length as nums where counts[i] is the number of subarrays owned by index i.

Example: for [2, 1, 2] the six subarrays are owned like this: [2] (index 0), [1] (index 1), [2] (index 2), [2, 1] (index 0), [1, 2] (index 2) and [2, 1, 2] (index 0), so the answer is [3, 1, 2].
hints: Index i owns a subarray [l, r] only if l ≤ i ≤ r and nothing in the subarray beats nums[i]. How far can l go to the left and r to the right?
Because the leftmost maximum owns the subarray, the elements to the left of i inside the subarray must be strictly smaller, and the elements to the right must be smaller or equal.

Let L be the nearest index to the left with nums[L] ≥ nums[i] and R the nearest index to the right with nums[R] > nums[i] (use -1 and n when there is none). Then counts[i] = (i - L) * (R - i). Find L and R for all indices with monotonic stacks.
editorial: Fix an index i and ask which subarrays it owns. A subarray [l, r] containing i is owned by i exactly when every element to the left of i in the subarray is strictly smaller than nums[i] and every element to the right is at most nums[i]. The left end can therefore be anything strictly after the nearest index L on the left holding a value ≥ nums[i], and the right end anything strictly before the nearest index R on the right holding a value > nums[i]. The choices are independent, so counts[i] = (i - L) * (R - i).

The asymmetric comparison (≥ on one side, > on the other) is what makes every subarray have exactly one owner; the counts always add up to n(n+1)/2. Both nearest-bigger indices come from a monotonic stack: scan left to right popping smaller values for L, and right to left popping smaller-or-equal values for R. Each index is pushed and popped once, so the total time is O(n). This contribution view, counting for each element how many subarrays it decides, is the basis of sum-of-subarray-minimums style problems.
solution:
def ownershipCounts(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    left = [-1] * n    # nearest index on the left with value >= nums[i]
    right = [n] * n    # nearest index on the right with value > nums[i]
    stack = []
    for i in range(n):
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < nums[i]:
            stack.pop()
        left[i] = stack[-1] if stack else -1
        stack.append(i)
    stack = []
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] <= nums[i]:
            stack.pop()
        right[i] = stack[-1] if stack else n
        stack.append(i)
    return [(i - left[i]) * (right[i] - i) for i in range(n)]
